<meta>This page continues the account of the Getae, a Thracian people who believe in immortality. The previous page ended with a description of their ritual sacrifice, where they hurl a chosen messenger onto spear-points to communicate with their god, Salmoxis.</meta>

<page-num>296</page-num>

->**HERODOTUS**<-

...upward toward the sky they shoot arrows and threaten the god, believing that there is no other god but their own.

95. Now, according to what I have heard from the Greeks who live by the Hellespont and the Black Sea, this Salmoxis <note>Also spelled Zalmoxis; he is a legendary figure who served as both a social reformer and a deity for the Getae.</note> was actually a mortal man who lived as a slave in Samos; he was a slave to Pythagoras, the son of Mnesarchus. After gaining his freedom there and acquiring great wealth, he returned to his own country. Because the Thracians led such impoverished lives and were somewhat simple-minded, this Salmoxis—who was well-acquainted with the Ionian <note>The Ionians were known for their intellectual advancements and luxury compared to the "barbarian" tribes.</note> way of life and possessed deeper customs than the Thracians, having associated with Greeks and especially with Pythagoras (a teacher <note>original: "sophistē," which at this time referred to a master of wisdom or a philosopher rather than the later negative connotation of a "sophist."</note> of no small reputation)—had a hall built for men. In this hall, he would host the leading citizens and, while entertaining them with banquets, he would teach them that neither he, nor his guests, nor any of their descendants would ever truly die, but would instead go to a place where they would live forever and possess every good thing. While he was carrying out these activities and speaking these words, he was meanwhile constructing an underground chamber. When the chamber was completely finished, he vanished from the sight of the Thracians; he went down into the underground room and lived there for three years. The Thracians longed for him and mourned him as if he were dead, but in the fourth year, he reappeared to them, and in this way they came to believe the things Salmoxis had told them. This is the story of what he did.

96. As for me, I neither disbelieve the story of this man and his underground chamber, nor do I believe it entirely; however, I suspect that this Salmoxis lived many years before Pythagoras. But whether...

<meta>This page continues the account of the Getae (a Thracian tribe) and their belief in immortality. It specifically transitions from their ritual practices to a Greek rationalization of their god, Salmoxis, as a former student of Pythagoras.</meta>

<page-num>297</page-num>

<header>BOOK IV. 94-96</header>

Thracians shoot arrows skyward as a threat to the god, believing in no other god but their own.

95. For myself, I have been told by the Greeks who dwell beside the Hellespont <note>The narrow strait connecting the Aegean Sea to the Sea of Marmara, now known as the Dardanelles.</note> and the Pontus <note>original: "Pontos," referring to the Black Sea.</note> that this Salmoxis was actually a human being who was once a slave in Samos; his master was Pythagoras, the son of Mnesarchus <note>The famous Greek philosopher and mathematician known for his theories on the transmigration of souls.</note>. Eventually, after being granted his freedom and accumulating great wealth, he returned to his own country. Now, the Thracians were a people who lived quite simply and were somewhat naive, but this Salmoxis had become acquainted with Ionian <note>Referring to the Greek inhabitants of Ionia, who were regarded as the most intellectually advanced and culturally sophisticated of the Greeks.</note> customs and a more refined way of life than what was found in Thrace. Because he had associated with Greeks—and specifically with one of the most powerful Greek teachers, Pythagoras—he commissioned the building of a hall. In this hall, he would entertain and provide banquets for the leading citizens of his country. During these feasts, he would teach them that neither he, nor his guests, nor any of their descendants would ever truly die; instead, they would go to a place where they would live forever in a state of total blessedness. While he was hosting these gatherings and teaching this doctrine, he was secretly constructing an underground chamber. When it was finished, he vanished from the sight of the Thracians and descended into this subterranean room. He lived there for three years, while the Thracians missed him and mourned him as if he were dead. Then, in the fourth year, he appeared to the Thracians again, and in this way, they came to believe the things Salmoxis had told them. Such is the story the Greeks tell about him.

excipient anni consequentes. Anno ante me censorem mortuus est, novem annis post meum consulatum, cum consul iterum me consule creatus esset. Num igitur, si ad centesimum annum vixisset, senectutis eum suae paeniteret? Nec enim excursione nec saltu, nec eminus hastis aut comminus gladiis uteretur, sed consilio ratione sententia, quae nisi essent in senibus, non summum consilium maiores nostri appellassent senatum. Apud Lacedaemonios quidem ei, qui amplissimum magistratum gerunt, ut sunt, sic etiam nominantur, senes. Quod si legere aut audire voletis externa, maximas res publicas ab adulescentibus labefactatas, a senibus sustentatas et restitutas reperietis.

Cedo qui vestram rem publicam tantam amisistis tam cito? sic enim percontantur<note>1 ut est after percontantur in MSS., generally omitted by editors.</note> in Naevi poetae Lupo.<note>2 Lupo Ribbeck, Bennett, Mommsen; Ludo MSS.</note> Respondentur et alia et hoc in primis :

proveniebant oratores novi, stulti adulescentuli.

Temeritas est videlicet florentis aetatis, prudentia senescentis.

# CICERO

years will follow in succession. He died the year before I was censor, nine years after my consulship, when he had been elected consul a second time while I was consul. If, therefore, he had lived to his hundredth year, would he regret his old age? He would not be using it for running, leaping, throwing spears from a distance, or fighting hand-to-hand with swords, but for counsel, reason, and opinion—qualities which, if they were not found in old men, our ancestors would not have called their highest deliberative body the <term>senatus</term> <gloss>senate, derived from the word for "old men"</gloss>. Among the Lacedaemonians, indeed, those who hold the highest magistracy are called, as they are in fact, elders. If you wish to read or hear of foreign affairs, you will find that the greatest states have been weakened by the young and sustained and restored by the old.

"How, pray, have you lost your great state so quickly?"
So they ask in the *Lupus* <gloss>Wolf</gloss> of the poet Naevius. They receive various answers, but this one in particular:

"New orators were coming forth, silly young lads."

Rashness is the mark of the blooming age, prudence that of the aging.

year will receive his memory and pass it on. He died in the year before I was censor, nine years after I was consul; and while I was holding the latter office he was elected consul for the second time. If, then, he had lived to his hundredth year, would he be repenting of his old age? No, for he would not be employing his time in running and in leaping, or in long-distance throwing of the spear, or in hand-to-hand sword-play, but he would be engaged in using reflection, reason, and judgement. If these mental qualities were not characteristic of old men our fathers would not have called their highest deliberative body the "senate."<note>1</note> Among the Lacedaemonians, for example, those who fill their chief magistracies are called "elders," as they are in fact. And indeed, if you care to read or hear foreign history, you will find that the greatest states have been overthrown by the young and sustained and restored by the old.

How lost you, pray, your mighty state so soon?

for such is the question put in a play entitled the *Wolf*, by the poet Naevius. Several answers are given, but the one chiefly in point is this:

> Through swarms of green, declaiming, silly lads.

True enough, for rashness is the product of the budding-time of youth, prudence of the harvest-time of age.
